vulgar.e: From Middle English vulgare, from Latin vulgāris, from volgus, vulgus (“mob; common folk”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH-. Compare Welsh gwala (“plenty, sufficiency”), Ancient Greek ἁλία (halía, “assembly”), εἰλέω (eiléō, “to compress”), Proto-Slavic *valъ.

s.d: (derogatory, historical) A common, ordinary person.
x: Popular antiquarian writings […] frequently focused on the regional vulgars' superstitious beliefs regarding the dead and their ongoing presence—such as popular funeral rites or the vulgars' fear of church yards.

s.d: The common people.
The language of a people, especially the commoners.
x: Therefore you Clowne, abandon: which is in the vulgar, leaue the societie: which in the boorish, is companie, of this female: which in the common, is woman: which together, is, abandon the society of this Female, […]

s.d: lacking refinement or cultivation or taste
x: he had coarse manners but a first-rate mind
behavior that branded him as common

s.d: of or associated with the great masses of people

behavior that branded him as common

s.d: Debased; uncouth; distasteful; obscene.

It might be more useful to the English reader […] to write in our vulgar language.

s.d: Common, usual; of the typical kind.
x: vulgar bush brown (Bicyclus vulgaris)

s.d: Being a vulgar fraction.
x: A fraction is vulgar if it has one integer divided by another integer, as long as the integer that's doing the dividing isn't equal to zero.

vulgarian.e: From vulgar + -ian. Compare Late Latin vulgārius, Latin vulgāris.

s.d: a vulgar person (especially someone who makes a vulgar display of wealth)
A vulgar individual, especially one who emphasizes or is oblivious to his or her vulgar qualities.
x: He was by this time on the deck, but he had the art to be quite unapproachable; the friendliest vulgarian, three parts drunk, would have known better than take liberties...

“There is another man in my life.”
Now, these are ugly words for a husband to hear. They dazed me, I confess. To beat her up in the street, there and then, as an honest vulgarian might have done, was not feasible.

s.d: Having the characteristics of a vulgarian, vulgar.
x: Your vulgarian friend is downstairs, denting innocent people's fenders.

x: We never descended to the vulgarism of a quarrel. People said that neither of us had a heart, but it appears to me that politeness is an excellent substitute.

vulpine.e: Borrowed from Latin vulpīnus (“foxy, fox-like”), from vulpēs, earlier volpēs (“fox”), from Proto-Indo-European *wl(o)p- (“fox”). Cognate with Welsh llywarn (“fox”), Ancient Greek ἀλώπηξ (alṓpēx), Armenian աղուէս (aġuēs), Albanian dhelpër, Lithuanian vilpišỹs (“wildcat”), Sanskrit लोपाश (lopāśa, “jackal, fox”).

s.d: Any of certain canids called foxes (including true foxes, arctic foxes and grey foxes), distinguished from canines, which are regarded as similar to dogs and wolves.
x: The family Canidae^([sic]) consists of two main subgroups, the vulpines (foxes) and the canines (wolves, coyotes, jackals, and dogs), and some intermediate “fox-dog” forms from South America.

s.d: A person considered cunning.
resembling or characteristic of a fox
x: vulpine cunning

s.d: Pertaining to a fox.
x: She dared not raise her eyes above the level of the tea-table, and she almost expected to see a spot of accusing vulpine blood drip down and stain the whiteness of the cloth.

s.d: Having the characteristics of a fox; foxlike; cunning.

vulture.e: Borrowed into Middle English from Anglo-Norman vultur, from Old French voutoir, voutre, from Latin vultur, voltur. Displaced native Old English ūf.

s.d: any of various large diurnal birds of prey having naked heads and weak claws and feeding chiefly on carrion
someone who attacks in search of booty
Any of several carrion-eating birds of the families Accipitridae and Cathartidae.
x: In clusters on the plain, like cowlless monks at matins, sat the vultures that had settled on the corpse of the hyena impaled by the female rhino […]

s.d: (colloquial, figuratively) A person who profits from the suffering of others.
x: Within ten minutes of the accident, the vultures appeared and were organizing lawsuits.

s.d: (colloquial, figuratively) To circle around one's target as if one were a vulture.
x: Rudy vultured when asking the girl out.

s.d: (obsolete) ravenous; rapacious
x:
Whose vultur thought doth pitch the price so hie,
That she will draw his lips rich treasure drie.

s.d: living by preying on other animals especially by catching living prey
x: a predatory bird
the rapacious wolf

s.d: Pertaining to or having characteristics of vultures.
x: Somewhat below the middle height, he was lean of body and vulturine of face.
Taking the cooked bird in her gnarled hands she stripped off the flesh with the few teeth she still had left in her head, gnawing on it with a vulturine concentration until it was just grey bones.

s.d: Predaceous.
x: A species of crow in vast numbers is generally found to attend the larger kind of birds of prey. It is uncommonly bold and ravenous, and all its habits are vulturine […]

vulva.e: Learned borrowing from Latin vulva, earlier volva (“womb, female sexual organ”), probably from volvō (“to turn, wrap around”). Akin to Sanskrit उल्ब॑ (úlba) and उल्व॑ (úlva, “womb”) or English valve, valva and other descendants of the Latin term (evolve, involve, revolve).

s.d: external parts of the female genitalia
The external female genitalia of humans and other placental mammals, which includes the clitoris, labia, and vulval vestibule/vulvar opening.
x: The vulvae of the sow were popular as a gourmet's dish. Credited with erotic effects.
The wedge-shaped character was the triangle, the archaic Paleolithic sign of the vulva; the pubic triangle was at the end of the phallic stylus.

s.d: A protrusion on the side of a nematode.
of or relating to the vulva
Of or pertaining to the vulva.
x: In John and Salomé, Salomé's nipples are angry blossoms, her black navel vulval, tendrilous, vaguely insectimorphic.
Pythagoras, she suggests, venerated three-sided figures for their vaginal symbolism; Upper Palaeolithic dips in rock are chipped away by cavemen into vulval icons.
